analysis.one_liner: Raises the minimum wage to $6.15 in steps and then adjusts it automatically for inflation.
analysis.headline: The bill to raise the minimum wage to $6.15 and index it to inflation was sent to a House committee and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have raised the federal minimum wage from $5.15 to $6.15 an hour in three yearly steps, and then, starting in 2002, automatically adjusted it each year for inflation so it would stop losing value in real terms. The bill never received a vote in the House committee or subcommittee it was sent to, and died when the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Roughly 10 million workers earning near the minimum wage would see their pay rise directly, and automatic inflation indexing would protect the raise from being eroded in future years without requiring new legislation.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage from $5.15 to $5.55, $5.85, and then $6.15 an hour over three years starting September 1, 1999.
After 2002, adjusts the wage each year for inflation (capped at 4% per year, never falling), so it would no longer erode between congressional pay-raise fights.

analysis.who_pays: Employers of minimum-wage workers — especially restaurants, retail, and small businesses — would bear higher payroll costs, and some could pass them to consumers in higher prices.

drawbacks.text: Raising the minimum wage to $6.15 and then indexing it to inflation would raise labor costs for employers, particularly small businesses that pay many minimum-wage jobs; some businesses could respond by cutting hours, raising prices, or slowing hiring.
The 4 percent annual cap on inflation adjustments means that in high-inflation years the minimum wage could still lose real value relative to prices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The modest increases and inflation indexing were a sensible, widely supported design that would have ended the biennial political fight over the minimum wage; the drawbacks were the mild cost to small businesses and the historically modest target level. Since the bill never even received a subcommittee vote, no such costs were ever weighed — the public simply lost the benefit.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to a House committee and then a subcommittee, where it sat with no hearing or vote until the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Introduced March 3, 1999, with three cosponsors, and referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce.
On March 26, 1999, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, the usual last stop for labor bills that die without action.
No further action was taken before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

The debate over a minimum wage increase was eventually resolved outside this bill: separate legislation passed in 2000 raising the wage to $5.75 and $6.15 by 2002, but without the automatic inflation indexing this bill proposed.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who pay minimum wage kept the $5.15 floor without the scheduled increases or automatic inflation adjustments, and members of Congress kept the leverage of having to vote on wage hikes periodically rather than having them happen automatically.

for.name: Rep. Jack Quinn
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and made the case for a phased increase with automatic inflation adjustments.

for.name: 3 cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors of the bill.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.role: House GOP leadership and Education and the Workforce Committee majority
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled committee action or a floor vote on the bill, letting it die in the Workforce Protections Subcommittee.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a small bipartisan list (2 Republican and 1 Democratic cosponsors) and no recorded vote, so no partisan divide is measurable in the record; the bill simply died in committee.

industries.industry: Low-wage employers (retail, restaurants, and other service industries)
industries.note: The bill would have raised payroll costs for businesses that rely on minimum-wage workers, roughly $1 an hour per worker at the peak of the phase-in. Opponents in Congress and small-business lobbies routinely argued such increases cost jobs, though most research finds modest effects.
